cues_changed.old: The same trick proves that every polynomial has roots. Take one of degree n, starting with z to the n. On a huge circle, z to the n dwarfs the other terms. Picture z to the n as a walker going n times around zero, and the polynomial as a dog on a leash. The leash is shorter than the walker's distance from zero, so the dog circles zero n times too. So there are exactly n roots inside, counted by order.
cues_changed.new: The same trick proves that every nonconstant complex polynomial has roots. Divide by its leading coefficient, which leaves its roots unchanged. Now it starts with z to the n, for some positive integer n. On a huge circle, z to the n dwarfs the other terms. Picture z to the n as a walker going n times around zero, and the polynomial as a dog on a leash. The leash is shorter than the walker's distance from zero, so the dog circles zero n times too. So there are exactly n roots inside, counted by order.

cues_changed.old: Everything since came from one demand. The complex derivative must be the same from every direction. On an open region, that makes every small piece of the map a stretch and a turn. It lets boundary values decide the inside. It lets a loop count zeros and poles, and it turns a real integral into a sum of residues. It allows at most one extension to a given connected region, though not always everywhere, and along different paths a continuation can branch.
